findings.claim: A push/pull linkage (also called a reverse-motion linkage) reverses the direction of input motion - push in one end and the other end pulls out. The dfn repeats it: A linkage that reverses the direction of a push or pull force along a straight line.
findings.truth: A push/pull linkage keeps the output moving in the SAME direction as the input. The linkage that reverses input direction is the reverse-motion linkage, a different mechanism. The lesson merges the two and gives the wrong behaviour for the one the spec names.
findings.evidence: spec 3.1.5 Linkages: bell cranks, push/pull; Seneca Learning AQA GCSE D&T 1.5.3 Linkages - 'The push/pull linkage keeps the direction of motion the same for the input and the output' and 'The reverse motion linkage reverses the motion of the input and giving an opposite output motion'

findings.claim: Flashcard 2 asks 'Name the three smart materials in the AQA spec.'
findings.truth: Student-facing text must never name the exam board. The question works without the board name.
findings.evidence: house rule: no board naming in student-facing text

findings.claim: KC[1] 'What type of battery can be charged, discharged and charged again many times?' keys index 2 (Rechargeable (lithium-ion) battery) but offers 'Lead-acid battery' as a distractor.
findings.truth: A lead-acid battery is rechargeable - a car starter battery is recharged by the alternator on every journey - so the item has two correct answers and marks a true answer wrong. Replacing the distractor with a single-use cell (silver oxide button cell) keeps the keyed index at 2.
findings.evidence: settled battery chemistry; the lesson's own glossary defines a rechargeable battery as one that can be charged, discharged and charged again many times, which lead-acid satisfies. Same fix already live on the free-tier row sharing this slug.

findings.claim: KC[2] 'A cam and follower converts _____ motion into reciprocating motion.' keys index 2 (Rotary) but offers 'Circular' as a distractor.
findings.truth: The lesson's own key fact glosses rotary motion as 'rotary (circular)', so 'Circular' names the keyed answer and is marked wrong. 'Reciprocating' is one of the four spec motions and is plainly wrong in this stem.
findings.evidence: L5 key fact lists the four motions as linear (straight line), rotary (circular), reciprocating and oscillating; spec 3.1.5 names the same four. Same fix already live on the free-tier row sharing this slug.

findings.claim: nanomaterials - materials engineered at the atomic scale to achieve enhanced properties
findings.truth: Nanomaterials are engineered at the nanoscale, roughly 1 to 100 nanometres, which is larger than the atomic scale. The lesson's own dfn already gives the correct 'nanoscale (billionths of a metre)', and spec 3.1.3 sets no size, so no mark turns on it.
findings.evidence: the lesson's own data-def attribute; spec 3.1.3 lists nanomaterials without a size claim

findings.claim: Softwoods come from coniferous, evergreen trees and grow faster, making them cheaper. Examples: larch ...
findings.truth: Larch is a deciduous conifer - it drops its needles each autumn - so 'evergreen' is not true of every softwood. The defining rule is coniferous, which the sentence already gives, and the spec lists larch as a softwood, so nothing examinable is at risk.
findings.evidence: spec 3.1.6.1 lists larch under softwoods; settled botany of Larix

findings.claim: the invention of graphene leading to new ultra-strong, lightweight products
findings.truth: Graphene was isolated from graphite in 2004 by Geim and Novoselov - a discovery and an isolation process, not an invention. Spec 3.1.3 itself frames modern materials as coming from the invention of new or improved processes, so the wording matches board language and costs no marks.
findings.evidence: spec 3.1.3 wording; settled history of graphene isolation

findings.claim: Temperature sensors (thermistors) detect temperature changes. Their resistance decreases as temperature rises. - repeated in the dfn, KC[3], flashcard 5 and the glossary.
findings.truth: This holds for NTC thermistors only; a PTC thermistor gains resistance as it warms. NTC is the type taught and used in GCSE systems work, so the statement matches board teaching material and needs no edit.
findings.evidence: spec 3.1.4 lists temperature sensors without specifying the coefficient; standard GCSE D&T teaching

findings.claim: Use the correct technical vocabulary - reciprocating not up and down, fulcrum not pivot point.
findings.truth: Pivot is accepted vocabulary for the fixed point of a lever, so the tip overstates the case. A student who follows it and writes fulcrum loses nothing, so the risk is one-way and an edit is not warranted.
findings.evidence: spec 3.1.5 Changing magnitude and direction of force; common D&T usage of pivot and fulcrum as interchangeable

summary: Six lessons checked against AQA Design and Technology 8552 section 3.1. One HIGH: L5 teaches the push/pull linkage as a reverse-motion linkage, inverting the behaviour of one of the two linkages the spec names. Two multiple-choice items carry a second correct answer among the distractors, and one flashcard names the exam board. Everything else verified sound: lever orders and their force/distance trade-offs, cam and follower, gear ratio (60:20 = 3:1, driven three times slower with three times the torque), pulley belt directions, bell crank at 90 degrees, the four motions, ferrous/non-ferrous/alloy, thermoforming/thermosetting, smart versus modern material classification, the physical/working property split, and the Section A exam claims (20 marks, multiple choice and short answer, 1-2 mark recall).
